                                       BEFORE THE

 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.                           )            Docket Nos. EL25-49-002

      REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, REHEARING
                            OF VISTRA CORP.

             Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Rules 212 and 713 of the

Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or

“FERC”),2 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) requests clarification, or in the alternative, rehearing, of the

order issued by the Commission on June 18, 2026, in the above-captioned dockets (“June 2026

Order”).3 The Commission should clarify one narrow issue: when a secondary generator4 in a

Co-Location Arrangement will continue to be available to PJM as a capacity resource and comply

with its Day-Ahead Market offer requirement, that unit should not be required to delist its Capacity




      1
          16 U.S.C. § 825l(a).
      2
          18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.713.
      3
          PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 (2026) (“June 2026 Order”).
      4
      In this context, a “secondary generator” refers to a generation unit that will serve the Co-Located Load only if
the unit dedicated to providing primary service to the Co-Located Load is on an outage and only if the secondary
generator is not committed in PJM’s energy market. However, Vistra notes that the same principles apply where the
service to the Co-Located Load does not come entirely from a single unit, but instead comes from portions of each
generation unit with the remaining MW from each unit being offered in PJM’s energy market.
 Interconnection Rights (“CIRs”). This clarification is necessary because the Commission’s June

2026 Order’s findings on CIR treatment did not address the circumstance in which the secondary

generator complies with the Day-Ahead Market offer requirement. To the extent this clarification

is denied, we seek rehearing.

               SPECIFICATION OF ERRORS & STATEMENT OF ISSUES

1. The PJM tariff is ambiguous as to whether an Interconnection Customer must delist the CIRs
   of a secondary, interruptible unit that serves a Co-Located Load only when not committed in
   the PJM market. The Commission should clarify that the PJM tariff does not require an
   Interconnection Customer to delist the CIRs of a unit of a capacity resource that is capable of
   meeting both the emergency performance and the Day-Ahead Market must-offer requirements
   applicable to capacity resources, if the unit provides secondary, interruptible service to a Co-
   Located Load only when the unit is not committed in PJM’s energy market. Without
   clarification, the PJM tariff violates the FPA requirement that rates, terms, and conditions of
   Commission-jurisdictional service be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or
   preferential. See 16 U.S.C. §§ 824d(a), 824d(b), 824e.

2. If the Commission declines to provide the clarification requested above, the June 2026 Order
   is arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, because the
   Commission failed to engage in reasoned decisionmaking by failing to respond to Vistra’s
   objections to PJM’s proposal and failing to consider the important issues that Vistra raised.
   See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Ins.
   Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983) (“State Farm”); Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015); Del. Div. of
   Pub. Advoc. v. FERC, 3 F.4th 461 (D.C. Cir. 2021); New England Power Generators Ass’n v.
   FERC, 881 F.3d 202 (D.C. Cir. 2018); TransCanada Power Mktg. Ltd. v. FERC, 811 F.3d 1
   (D.C. Cir. 2015); Pub. Serv. Comm’n of Ky. v. FERC, 397 F.3d 1004 (D.C. Cir. 2005);
   Canadian Ass’n of Petroleum Producers v. FERC, 254 F.3d 289, 299 (D.C. Cir. 2001).

3. If the Commission declines to provide the clarification requested above, the June 2026 Order
   is arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, because the
   Commission accepted tariff provisions that did not comply with its directive to clarify its
   interconnection procedures and agreements to increase certainty and consistency. See 5 U.S.C.
   § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. 29; FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502
   (2009); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 159 (2025).

4. If the Commission declines to provide the clarification requested above, the June 2026 Order
   is arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act and the Federal
   Power Act, to the extent the Commission accepted unjust, unreasonable, and unduly
   discriminatory tariff provisions that require a secondary, interruptible unit serving Co-Located
   Load only when not committed in PJM’s market (and only when the primary unit is not serving
   the Co-Located Load) to delist its CIRs to implement a Co-Location Arrangement. See
   5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); 16 U.S.C. §§ 824d, 824e; State Farm, 463 U.S. 29.

 I.       Background

                Last December, the Commission found that the PJM tariff is unjust and unreasonable

     because it lacks sufficient clarity and consistency regarding how interconnection customers can

     serve Co-Located Load using existing generating facilities.5 The Commission directed PJM to

     propose tariff revisions to clarify that existing generators can use the necessary study process to

     modify their interconnection to reflect the addition of new Co-Located Loads.6 In connection with

     the addition of those Co-Located Loads, the Commission explained that “an existing generating

     facility may not begin serving Co-Located Load that is not Network Load until it has delisted its

     CIRs for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve any Co-Located Load that

     is not receiving [Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”)].”7

                PJM proposed, on compliance, to require existing generators that seek to serve Co-Located

     Load to submit to PJM “the amount of reduction to [CIRs] to facilitate the Co-Located Load

     configuration.”8 PJM would then “assess the impact of the reduction in [CIRs]” in the necessary

     study process.9

                Vistra filed a protest to PJM’s compliance filing, expressing concern that this tariff

     language remained ambiguous and therefore did not address the Commission’s directive to

     “clarify” its interconnection procedures to ensure that it is clear to existing generators how to

tariff language was ambiguous with regards to how a generator should calculate the amount by

which its CIRs should be reduced. Vistra expressed concern that the tariff could be read to require

generators to delist CIRs associated with any facility that would ever provide power to Co-Located

Load, not just the portion of the facility designated to serve the Co-Located Load. Under this

broad reading, an existing, two-unit generator with one 50 MW unit serving Co-Located Load on

a firm basis and one 50 MW unit serving Co-Located Load on an interruptible, secondary basis

only when the unit is not committed in PJM’s energy market would need to delist 100 MWs of

CIRs. In other words, the generator would need to delist more CIRs than the portion the facility

designated to serve the Co-Located Load on a firm basis.11

          Vistra explained that this overly broad reading would be unduly discriminatory. There is

no principled basis to treat a secondary unit in a Co-Location Arrangement differently from a

generator with a non-firm or recallable commitment to sell power outside of PJM where both types

of generators comply with all capacity resource obligations, including the Day-Ahead Market

must-offer requirement.12 And as a matter of policy, there is no reason to ignore the valuable

contribution secondary units can make to resource adequacy. Doing so would unnecessarily

deprive the PJM region of available capacity.13

            In the June 2026 Order, the Commission summarized some of Vistra’s arguments14 but did

not meaningfully respond to them. It simply “disagree[d] with Vistra and Constellation that

capacity resources should not have to reduce their CIRs to serve Co-Located Load.”15 Its sole

support for this conclusion was a cross-reference to its reasoning in an earlier section of the June

2026 Order, where it had addressed Constellation’s argument—which was distinct from any of

Vistra’s arguments in critical ways. Specifically, Constellation argued that a generator serving

Co-Located Load should retain its CIRs if “PJM can verify that the Co-Located Load has no

contractual right to energy from the generator during a capacity emergency and that the Co-

Located Load has the ability either to curtail or draw on back-up power.”16 In that earlier section

of the June 2026 Order, the Commission rejected Constellation’s argument, explaining that under

the scenario Constellation laid out, “the Co-Located Generator would not be capable of meeting

its entire capacity requirement,” which includes the requirement to offer its energy into the Day-

Ahead Market throughout the delivery year. It found that Constellation’s proposal would allow

the capacity resource to violate the must-offer requirement and thus provide an inferior capacity

product for the same payment.17

 II.   Request for Clarification

             Clarification of the June 2026 Order is necessary because it accepted unclear tariff

  language and failed to explain how that tariff language applies to the issue Vistra raised in its

  protest. Specifically, the December 2025 Order found that existing generators need only delist

  CIRs “for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve any Co-Located Load that

  is not receiving NITS.”18 PJM’s compliance filing failed to account for this specific Commission

  directive, instead generally leaving it to generators to submit “the amount of reduction to [CIRs]

  to facilitate the Co-Located Load configuration,”19 without specifying how that CIR reduction

  should be calculated. Rather than direct PJM to remedy that ambiguity in a manner consistent

  with the December 2025 Order, the Commission accepted PJM’s vague language and did not

  respond to the nuances of how that language should apply.

             PJM’s tariff revisions—and the Commission order accepting them—are ambiguous on the

  critical point of how customers should calculate the reduction in CIRs. PJM’s tariff language risks

  being interpreted far too broadly, to require an Interconnection Customer to delist the CIRs for a

  capacity resource that is capable of meeting both the emergency performance and the Day-Ahead

  Market must-offer requirements, and that provides secondary, interruptible service to a Co-

  Located Load only when the unit is not committed in PJM’s energy market. Vistra respectfully

  requests that the Commission clarify that PJM’s tariff revisions should not be read in that manner.

  The Commission should clarify that an Interconnection Customer is not required to delist the

           December 2025 Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 230 (emphasis added).
      19

 portion of the CIRs that meet the specifications described above when implementing a Co-

Location Arrangement.

           As discussed below, Vistra’s requested interpretation is consistent with the December 2025

Order. It is also consistent with the rest of the PJM tariff. Moreover, allowing this ambiguity to

persist (or adopting a contrary interpretation) would be unjust and unreasonable and unduly

discriminatory or preferential.

           A. Vistra’s Requested Clarification Is Consistent With the December 2025 Order
              and the Reasoning in the June 2026 Order

           The Commission’s December 2025 Order set a clear standard: an existing generator must

delist CIRs “for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve any Co-Located

Load that is not receiving NITS.”20 PJM’s compliance proposal did not clearly implement that

standard.

           To “designate” something is “to indicate and set [it] apart for a specific purpose, office, or

duty.”21 In the configuration Vistra described in its protest, a portion of the generating facility is

clearly “set apart for [the] specific purpose” of serving the Co-Located Load. The remainder of

the facility is not. The facility will continue offering the remaining generation into the Day-Ahead

Market and injecting power onto the PJM grid when it receives a Day-Ahead Market award.

Accordingly, the remaining capacity is not “designated” to serve the Co-Located Load, which

means that under the December 2025 Order, it need not delist its CIRs.

2026); accord Designate, Black’s Law Dictionary (12th ed. 2024) (“To choose (someone or something) for a particular
job or purpose.”).

                                                       -7-
            The Commission’s June 2026 Order did not address this issue. Rather, it addressed

Constellation’s (different) argument that a capacity resource serving Co-Located Load that can

supply power to the grid during emergencies should not be required to delist its CIRs. The

Commission’s reason for rejecting Constellation’s argument was that such a resource would be

incapable of meeting its Day-Ahead Market must-offer obligation.22 That reasoning simply does

not apply to the scenario Vistra presented, where the secondary, interruptible unit would meet its

Day-Ahead Market must-offer obligation and would only serve Co-Located Load if doing so did

not conflict with its commitment in PJM’s market (and would only do so as backup to the primary

unit which is designated to serve the Co-Located Load). The Commission should clarify that these

types of secondary units—that meet Day-Ahead Market must-offer requirements—should retain

their CIRs.

           B. Clarification Will Ensure that the PJM Tariff Is Just and Reasonable and Not
              Unduly Discriminatory or Preferential

           Vistra’s requested clarification will ensure compliance with the FPA. As Vistra explained

in its protest, requiring a secondary, interruptible unit that serves Co-Located Load only when it is

not committed in PJM’s market (and only when the primary unit is not serving the Co-Located

Load) to delist its CIRs would be unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory or

preferential.23

           PJM already permits a class of resources with non-firm, non-network commitments to

participate as capacity resources: generators with a non-firm or recallable commitments to external

sales of capacity. While the tariff excuses capacity resources with firm commitments to external




    22
         See June 2026 Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 161.
    23
         16 U.S.C. § 824

                                                       -8-
 sales of their capacity from the capacity market must-offer requirement,24 it does not excuse

capacity resources with non-firm or recallable commitments to external sales from that

requirement.25 The tariff thus recognizes that firm external sales pose unique concerns for meeting

capacity market commitments, while non-firm or recallable external sales do not: generators with

non-firm or recallable external sale commitments can be expected to perform normally in the

capacity market. The same distinction applies here. Primary units that provide firm energy to a

Co-Located Load clearly cannot also meet the obligations of PJM capacity resources, but

secondary units that provide interruptible, backup energy to a Co-Located Load can.

         There is no principled basis to treat a secondary, interruptible unit in a Co-Location

Arrangement differently from an external resource with a non-firm capacity commitment. Like

generators with non-firm or recallable external sale commitments, secondary interruptible units

can fulfill capacity resource obligations.26 Accordingly, the two classes of generators are similarly

situated with respect to their ability to serve as capacity resources. Subjecting the two categories

to different rules—specifically, allowing one to maintain CIRs while requiring the other to delist

them—would amount to undue discrimination.

         Further, it would be unjust and unreasonable to require a secondary, interruptible unit

serving Co-Located Load only when not committed in PJM’s market (and only when the primary

unit is not serving the Co-Located Load) to delist its CIRs to implement a Co-Location

secondary unit would be fully capable of meeting PJM’s capacity commitment requirements—

including both the emergency performance requirement and the Day-Ahead Market must-offer

obligation.

           Requiring that secondary, interruptible unit to delist its CIRs would deprive the PJM

capacity market of available capacity for no conceivable reason.27 For the vast majority of hours,

the secondary, interruptible unit could offer into the Day-Ahead Market and provide energy when

economic. In the remaining hours, the secondary, interruptible unit could offer into the Day-Ahead

such that the unit would be available to the system during emergencies. Such a resource has all

the hallmarks of a capacity resource. It is patently unjust and unreasonable to deprive the capacity

market of such a resource at a time when capacity market supply is tight, demand is rising, and

PJM and the Commission face unprecedented pressure to address rising prices.28

           In addition, forcing the secondary unit to delist its CIRs would disincentivize the Co-

Located Load from providing demand response to the grid. Because the Co-Located Load would

have to pay for the secondary unit’s capacity, there would be no reason for the Co-Located Load

to choose to switch to its own back-up generator and make the secondary unit’s capacity available

to the grid.

               The Commission should grant clarification that secondary, interruptible units in the

   scenario Vistra has outlined are not required to delist their CIRs. This clarification would comport

   with the December 2025 Order, and it would ensure that the PJM tariff remains just and reasonable

   and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

III.   Alternative Request for Rehearing

              To the extent the Commission denies the clarification Vistra seeks above, Vistra requests

   rehearing of the June 2026 Order.          In the absence of Vistra’s requested clarification, the

   Commission’s decision in the June 2026 Order was arbitrary, capricious, and otherwise not in

   accordance with law for three reasons.29 First, the Commission failed to respond to any of the

   objections Vistra raised on this issue in its protest. Second, the Commission erred in accepting a

   proposal that failed to comply with the Commission’s directive to “clarify” procedures for entering

   Co-Location Arrangements. Third, the Commission erred in accepting PJM’s proposal because it

   is unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory or preferential in violation of the Federal

   Power Act to the extent it requires secondary, interruptible units to delist their CIRs. For those

   reasons, the Commission’s acceptance of PJM’s proposal violated its obligation to engage in

   reasoned decisionmaking and its duty under the FPA to ensure that the rates, terms, and conditions

   of transmission service are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory. To remedy these

   flaws, the Commission should grant rehearing and direct PJM to revise its tariff to specify that a

   secondary, interruptible unit serving a Co-Located Load only when not committed in PJM’s

   markets is not required to delist its CIRs to implement a Co-Location Arrangement.

            A. The Commission’s Failure to Respond to Vistra’s Objections Was Arbitrary and
              Capricious

           The June 2026 Order does not reflect the type of reasoned decisionmaking required by the

Administrative Procedure Act.30 “It is well established” that the Administrative Procedure Act’s

reasoned decisionmaking standard means that the “Commission must respond meaningfully to the

arguments raised before it.”31 In responding to those arguments, the Commission may not “fail[]

to consider an important aspect of the problem” it addresses.32 The June 2026 Order summarily

dismissed Vistra’s arguments, without responding to them, by citing an inapposite discussion

about an entirely distinct argument. That is squarely in the zone of arbitrary and capricious

action.33

           As detailed above,34 Vistra’s protest raised four distinct arguments about PJM’s proposal

regarding reduction of CIRs. First, Vistra argued that PJM’s vague tariff language did not meet

the directive in the December 2025 Order to “clarify” its interconnection procedures and

agreements to ensure that existing generators know how to enter a Co-Location Arrangement.35

Rather than provide clarity, PJM’s proposal introduced ambiguity as to how CIR reductions should

Order. In that irrelevant discussion, the Commission found that a resource that “would not be

capable of meeting its entire capacity requirement,” including both its emergency performance

          By declining to engage with or respond to Vistra’s objections, and by instead citing

reasoning addressing a distinct issue, the Commission failed to “respond meaningfully to the

several important aspects of the issues the June 2026 Order addressed.44

          B. PJM’s Tariff Revisions Do Not Satisfy the Directive to “Clarify” its
             Interconnection Procedures

          In accepting PJM’s tariff revisions, the Commission departed from its directive in the

December 2025 Order to “clarify” its interconnection procedures.                 The Commission must

acknowledge and provide a reasoned explanation for a change in position.45                Because the

Commission failed to do so here, it erred in accepting PJM’s proposal.

          The fundamental problem that the Commission ordered PJM to remedy in the December

2025 Order was the tariff’s failure to address “with sufficient clarity or consistency” the rates,

terms, and conditions of service applicable to interconnection customers serving Co-Located Load.

These defects left customers “unable to determine what steps they must take to effectuate Co-

Location Arrangements,” leading to “uncertainty,” “disparate treatment,” and “no consistent

          As discussed above, PJM’s tariff language governing reduction of CIRs does not satisfy

reduction necessary to effectuate Co-Location Arrangements. Indeed, this vague language risks

being read far too broadly, to require generators to include in their CIR reduction calculation even

the CIRs associated with a secondary, interruptible unit, an unjust and unreasonable and unduly

discriminatory result.49 In other words, the lack of clarity in the tariff will lead to precisely the

types of problems the December 2025 Order told PJM to fix: uncertainty, disparate treatment, and

inconsistent understandings of customers’ responsibilities.

          Elsewhere in the June 2026 Order, the Commission rejected PJM’s proposed tariff

provisions when they contained insufficient detail to provide clarity to customers to ensure that

rates would be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.50 But PJM’s

tariff provisions addressing CIR reductions suffer from the same defect. The Commission

therefore erred in not directing PJM to address that defect with respect to CIRs.51

            C. It Is Unjust and Unreasonable and Unduly Discriminatory to Require a
              Secondary, Interruptible Unit to Delist its CIRs

           The FPA requires the Commission to ensure that rates, terms, and conditions for

jurisdictional services are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.52 The

Commission erred when it accepted PJM’s proposed tariff provisions because they violate that

foundational standard.

           As Vistra has explained, requiring a secondary, interruptible unit serving Co-Located Load

only when not committed in PJM’s market (and only when the primary unit is not serving the Co-

Located Load) to delist its CIRs to implement a Co-Location Arrangement is unjust and

unreasonable and unduly discriminatory or preferential, in violation of the FPA.

           First, as explained above,53 it is unduly discriminatory for PJM to require secondary,

interruptible units to delist their CIRs. The PJM tariff permits generators with non-firm, recallable

external sale commitments to serve as capacity resources.54 There is no principled distinction

between those resources and secondary, interruptible units that would justify prohibiting

secondary, interruptible units from also serving as capacity resources. Both types of generators

are similarly situated with respect to their ability to fulfill all capacity resource obligations and

their ability to perform when needed.55 Subjecting them to different rules—specifically, allowing

one to maintain CIRs but requiring the other to delist them—is impermissible undue

discrimination.

              Second, as explained above,56 it is unjust and unreasonable to require a secondary,

  interruptible unit serving Co-Located Load only when not committed in PJM’s market (and only

  when the primary unit is not serving the Co-Located Load) to delist its CIRs to implement a Co-

  Location Arrangement. This unit would be fully capable of meeting all of the performance

  requirements applicable to a capacity resource—including both the emergency performance

  requirement and the Day-Ahead Market must-offer obligation. Requiring it to delist its CIRs

  would deprive the PJM capacity market of available capacity at a time when PJM has no capacity

  to spare. Doing so would deprive the generation resource owner of its ability to provide capacity

  to PJM—and harm resource adequacy in PJM—for no conceivable reason, resulting in unjust and

  unreasonable rates.

IV.   Conclusion

             At a time when PJM’s capacity market is increasingly tight on supply, demand is rising

  rapidly, and PJM and the Commission face an affordability imperative, there is no reason to ignore

  the valuable contributions that secondary, interruptible units can make to resource adequacy and

  to affordability. Prohibiting these resources from supplying capacity to the PJM grid, when there

  is no technical or commercial limit on their ability to do so, will force PJM to procure unnecessary

  capacity.

             The Commission can readily prevent that outcome by granting clarification on the narrow

  issue Vistra presents. Thus, the Commission can and should grant clarification that PJM’s tariff

  should not be read to require an Interconnection Customer to delist the CIRs of a unit that provides

       In the alternative, the Commission should grant rehearing of its acceptance of PJM’s tariff

revisions regarding CIR reductions in the June 2026 Order. For the reasons discussed above,

requiring such a unit to delist its CIRs would be unjust and unreasonable and unduly

discriminatory. Accordingly, the Commission should grant rehearing and direct PJM to revise its
